title: Former DOJ Attorney Says Trump Antisemitism Probes at Universities Lacked Evidence
excerpt: A whistleblower complaint alleges the administration's investigations into Harvard, Columbia, and other schools had predetermined outcomes and ignored due process — raising stakes for thousands of Indian-American students.
body:
• A former career DOJ attorney filed a whistleblower complaint alleging that the Trump administration's antisemitism probes at major universities were marked by "predetermined outcomes" and lacked factual evidence.
  • The complaint, released by Rep. Jamie Raskin, says proposals to also investigate anti-Muslim bias on campuses were rejected by DOJ leadership.
  • Columbia University paid $200 million and Brown paid $50 million to settle federal probes, while Harvard continues to fight — a standoff with direct implications for Indian-American students and parents.

A former Department of Justice attorney has alleged that the Trump administration's high-profile investigations into antisemitism at American universities lacked evidence, had predetermined outcomes, and violated due process norms, according to a whistleblower complaint made public on Tuesday.

Haley Van Erem, a former career attorney in the DOJ's civil rights division, said through her lawyers that the probes conducted by the administration's Joint Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism were "marked by extraordinary procedural irregularities, predetermined outcomes without factual or legal support, and disregard" for legal requirements and free speech rights.

The complaint was sent to the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee and released by Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin.

What the Complaint Alleges

According to the filing, senior officials at the DOJ and the Department of Health and Human Services "departed from longstanding investigative practices designed to ensure due process, accuracy and legal compliance."

"For at least some of the investigations, there was little to no factual predicate justifying opening them," the complaint states. "When they asked questions, raised legal concerns, or sought to document their objections, they were sometimes admonished and their concerns were often disregarded."

"The mandate to conduct interviews with some Middle East studies professors seemed like an attempt to intimidate those professors and was rooted in Islamophobic assumptions rather than any actual evidence of complaints about antisemitism."

— Whistleblower complaint filed by Haley Van Erem's attorneys

The complaint also reveals that Van Erem and other DOJ attorneys proposed opening parallel investigations into anti-Muslim bias at universities, but those proposals "were not pursued by leadership."

A DOJ spokesperson pushed back, saying Van Erem "did not work on university investigations" and that "the department stands behind the integrity of these investigations."

The Crackdown on Universities

The Trump administration has targeted at least 10 major universities over alleged failures to protect Jewish students from discrimination, using Title VI of the Civil Rights Act — which prohibits discrimination in federally funded programs — as its primary legal tool. The government has threatened to withhold billions in federal funding from institutions that do not comply.

Columbia University reached a settlement in July 2025, agreeing to pay more than $200 million to the federal government and accepting conditions including tighter student discipline, screening of international students, and reviews of its Middle East studies programs. Brown University settled separately, paying $50 million for local workforce development.

Harvard University has refused to make a deal. The institution has characterized the administration's actions as "retaliatory" and a threat to "our independence and constitutional rights." A federal judge in Massachusetts dismissed the DOJ's antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard earlier this month, finding that the cited evidence was insufficient to support the claim.

The Campus Debate

The probes grew out of a wave of pro-Palestinian protests that swept American campuses following the start of Israel's war in Gaza in late 2023. The Trump administration alleges the protests crossed into antisemitism, while many protesters — including some Jewish groups — argue that opposing Israel's military operations is not the same as antisemitism.

The broader crackdown has expanded beyond antisemitism allegations. The government has also targeted universities over diversity initiatives, transgender policies, and climate programs, raising concerns from rights advocates about academic freedom and free speech.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

Tens of thousands of Indian-American students attend the universities under federal scrutiny, including Harvard, Columbia, Brown, UCLA, UC Berkeley, and NYU. The investigations — and the settlements universities have agreed to — can affect campus policies on international student admissions, academic program reviews, and the framework for student protest and political expression.

For Indian-American parents weighing elite university choices, the federal pressure campaign introduces a new variable: how institutions navigate government demands versus academic independence, and what that means for the campus environment their children will enter.

What Comes Next

The whistleblower complaint adds ammunition to Congressional Democrats' push to scrutinize the administration's university probes. The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights has opened its own sweeping investigation into the government's handling of campus antisemitism, sending formal requests for information to about a dozen schools.

Harvard's legal battle with the administration is ongoing. With the DOJ's lawsuit dismissed, the government will need to decide whether to appeal or pursue other avenues. The outcome will likely set the tone for how aggressively the administration can wield federal funding as leverage over higher education.
